newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin offers Russia concept of undivided nation.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin offers Russia concept of undivided nation.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, starting his return to political life after a marathon heart operation, marked Thursday's anniversary of the Bolshevik revolution by calling for national unity guided by a firm hand in the Kremlin.

"We are one nation," Yeltsin said in a statement issued from the intensive care ward where he is recovering from his seven hours of surgery. "We have one fate, one future. And we are all from the same past."
The 1917 revolution split Russia into warring factions.
"To this day, the nation is split into reds and whites, into us and them," Yeltsin said. "It is time to end this. We have one Russia and we must be together."
Yeltsin ordered that November 7, celebrated for 79 years as Revolution Day, should be renamed as a mark of remembrance for the victims of national discord and to promote civil peace.

"Keen not to allow confrontation in the future, in the interests of unity...I declare the November 7 holiday to be the Day of Accord and Reconciliation," Yeltsin's decree said. It also said 1997 would be the Year of Accord and Reconciliation.

While offering an olive branch to political foes in Moscow, Yeltsin made clear he would stamp on independent-minded regional leaders who tried to short-circuit the central authorities and rule their domains without reference to the capital.
He issued a decree introducing a system of watchdog bodies charged with enforcing the Kremlin's will anywhere in Russia.
Yeltsin, who sent tanks to quell a revolt by communist supporters of Russia's intractable Soviet-era parliament in 1993, has toned down his anti-communist rhetoric since then.

Anxious to avoid alienating millions of mainly elderly communist sympathisers, he lifted a ban on the flying the Red Flag during the 1995 celebrations of the 50th anniversary of the allied victory in World War Two.
And Yeltsin, once a member of the Soviet Politburo, has shown he can work with the present, communist-led parliament.

Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing on Thursday that the new holiday was an integral part of Yeltsin's new political concept, which he had been planning to put into action after his reelection in July.
"The idea of accord and reconciliation is central to the president's second term," Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing.

"The president is closing the era of discord and public cataclysm which ravaged the country for long years between 1905 and 1993. This is a step by a powerful president," he said, referring to the period between the first Russian revolution and the abortive hardline parliamentary revolt against Yeltsin.
Russia has changed dramatically after five years of economic and political reform putting it on the road to capitalism.
But bitter economic crisis, social upheaval and the loss of superpower status have stirred nostalgia among many Russians who associate the stability of the Soviet era with lost grandeur.

Attempts to dislodge mementoes of that time -- like Lenin's mummified body in a mausoleum on Red Square, the red stars atop the Kremlin towers or even the Soviet emblem on the parliament building -- have failed.
Yeltsin's new line is unlikely to please hard-core leftists, who held rallies across Russia on Thursday, or radical liberals.
The liberals want the Kremlin to brand the 1917 revolution as a crime against the nation. Radical communists say there can be no peace until communism is restored.

But moderate communist and reformist leaders, who form the bulk of Moscow's new establishment, seem keen to foster stability in a country in the face of huge financial problems and a growing threat of regional separatism.
As Yeltsin readied for surgery, aides campaigned to rein in leaders of Russia's 89 regions, many appointed by Yeltsin but showing signs of going their own way in the president's absence.
Many regional leaders hope to strengthen their positions after local polls which are now under way. Personal election victories will end many governors' dependence on the Kremlin.
Yeltsin's chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais has warned the regional bosses that any attempt to ignore Moscow's orders or avoid the Kremlin's control will be prosecuted.
